choice_assessments.reason: This is 0.10 × (0.60 × 800 + 0.40 × 150). It incorrectly treats the stated shares of large-fish energy as fractions of each prey population production used. The resulting contributions would be 48 and 6, whose shares are 88.9% and 11.1%, not 60% and 40%.
This is 10% of zooplankton production alone. It does not incorporate the required small-fish share or establish a minimum.

This is 10% of each entire prey production added together, 80 + 15. Those contributions have approximately 84.2% and 15.8% shares, incompatible with the stated 60% and 40% shares under the ordinary route accounting.
This repeats small-fish production. It is not large-fish production implied by the efficiencies or diet shares.

items.distractor_reason: Several numbers represent recognizable arithmetic errors, but the stem has no correct option and no specified lower bound; it therefore cannot supply three distractors around a warranted answer.
items.difficulty_reason: The subject matter requires reconciling two energy pathways, their production, efficiencies, and dietary shares. Those are multiple meaningful constraints, although their formulation here prevents a valid solution.
items.notes: If 10% is defined as actual route-specific receiving production divided by total prey production, the implied 80 and 15 contributions conflict with the diet shares. If it is instead an efficiency for available allocated prey energy, the shares impose capacity bounds: 0.60L <= 80 and 0.40L <= 15, so the limiting maximum is 37.5 kJ/m² under additional ordinary allocation assumptions. That is a maximum, not a minimum, and is absent. Production actually realized or its positive minimum is not specified. The small-fish pathway also originates from zooplankton, so adding both prey productions without an allocation account requires care. No listed minimum is warranted.

The stem supplies no rule authorizing distrust of either the ratio or the bar. Both conditional numerical results are reported, but neither is an unqualified solution.

choice_assessments.choice: Energy transfer efficiency from producers to consumers is approximately 10%
choice_assessments.reason: The directly calculable ratio is 400/5,000 = 8%, using total production summed across consumer levels. That is not a specified single trophic-level transfer efficiency. Approximately has no tolerance, so a loose interpretation might call 8% approximately 10%, but the stem does not warrant this as a precise, unambiguous conclusion.

choice_assessments.choice: The small producer biomass supports larger consumer biomass because producers replenish rapidly
choice_assessments.reason: Rapid producer turnover is a plausible standard explanation of inverted biomass pyramids, and is compatible with the observations. The snapshot plus annual energy production does not establish that causal explanation directly. Biomass energy content, turnover or persistence, and sufficient information about production and standing stock over time are not supplied.

choice_assessments.choice: Consumer biomass exceeding producer biomass violates the second law of thermodynamics
choice_assessments.reason: A standing-biomass comparison is not an energy-flow comparison. An inverted standing-biomass pyramid does not violate the second law.

choice_assessments.choice: Annual energy flow to consumers must exceed 5,000 kJ/m² to sustain 800 g/m² biomass
choice_assessments.reason: Standing grams do not determine an annual energy requirement without further information. The stated consumer production is 400 kJ/m² annually; neither it nor the biomass snapshot establishes the proposed lower bound on total energy flow.

items.distractor_reason: There is no unequivocally warranted listed conclusion. The 10% option also has vague approximation language, while the turnover option turns a compatible mechanism into a claimed demonstrated cause. The last two largely share the same stock-versus-flow confusion.
items.difficulty_reason: The learner must distinguish production over time from standing stock, recognize the difference between all-consumer totals and a trophic transfer, and distinguish a plausible mechanism from a conclusion established by observations.
items.notes: The data directly establish an inverted producer/shellfish standing-biomass comparison and an aggregate consumer-production to producer-production ratio of 8%. Neither exact statement is offered. I withhold approval rather than treat rapid replenishment as proven. There is residual ambiguity in how loosely approximately 10% and producers to consumers are intended; accepting that reading would itself undermine a unique intended inference about turnover.
